title: I think i have actually created a automated profitable trading edge, help!?
author: CantaloupeEast6276
selftext:
I've spent a considerable amount of time developing an automated trading bot for XAUUSD using cTrader, and I'd be interested to hear what experienced traders and algo developers think.

I've been through multiple versions, testing different risk settings and improvements, with backtesting covering approximately four years of historical tick data.

I'm keeping the actual strategy private, but here are some results from January–October 2026, starting with a 5,000 account balance.

1% equity risk:

* Net profit: +1,974
* Profit factor: 1.81
* Max balance drawdown: 2.96%
* Max equity drawdown: 4.52%
* Total trades: 186

1.5% equity risk:

* Net profit: +3,310
* Max equity drawdown: 8.20%

2% equity risk:

* Net profit: +6,085
* Profit factor: 1.75
* Max equity drawdown: 10.23%

I've also run 5,000 block-bootstrap Monte Carlo simulations to assess the robustness of the historical results, with simulated probabilities of reaching a predefined loss threshold ranging from 0.02% at 1% risk to 13.52% at 2% risk.

https://i.redd.it/wrglmuojtowh1.png

I actually took the bot live today on a real-money account.

It executed its first trade, which happened to be a loss. Afterwards, I ran a backtest covering that same trading day, and the results were almost identical.

The live trade entered at exactly the same price, with virtually identical execution timing, and the final P&L differed by just $0.12.

Obviously, one live trade proves very little, but it was encouraging to see the backtest and live execution match so closely.

I'm not selling anything, and I'm certainly not claiming I've cracked the markets. I'm simply trying to establish whether I've developed something with a sustainable statistical edge.

For anyone experienced with automated trading, what do you think?

Do these results look promising? What would you be looking for in terms of further validation, overfitting, drawdown and long-term robustness?

I'd genuinely appreciate some constructive feedback.

  
I have gone live today with a live trading account, it has taken 1 trade. I then backtested today and it produced the same result

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: a live fill matching the backtest to 12 cents on one quiet trade says the execution model is fine on a normal day. gold backtests usually lie on news candles, and a bootstrap of the same 186 trades can't show you one it never saw. does the bot sit out NFP and CPI or trade through them?

replies.author: CantaloupeEast6276
replies.body:
That's a very valid point, and something I definitely need to investigate further.

Currently, the bot doesn't have a dedicated economic news filter, so it can trade through NFP and CPI releases if they occur during its active trading window.

  
I've stress-tested historical results using different commission and slippage assumptions, but I appreciate that's not the same as accurately modelling the spread widening, liquidity gaps and unpredictable fills that can occur during major announcements.

I also completely agree regarding Monte Carlo. Resampling historical trades helps assess sequencing risk, but it can't account for market conditions or execution events that weren't represented in the original data.

Appreciate the feedback. These are exactly the weaknesses I'm trying to identify before scaling anything up.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: a calendar filter is cheap to test before you build it: drop every trade that opened within 30 minutes of a high-impact release and rerun. if the curve barely moves you lose nothing by adding it, and if half the edge disappears you've found out where it was coming from.

comments.author: Partnikl
comments.body:
Looks certainly good, and I'm happy for you if you've found something!

IMO, the elephant in the room is the January–October 2026 data. Was that actually untouched out-of-sample / forward testing? If not, there's a pretty big risk of overfitting.

Also, you mentioned four years of tick data, so how did the other years perform? January–October is a pretty short timeframe, potentially just one market regime.

I started with TSLA and NVDA strategies and had insanely good results for both. Then I expanded my testing to more historical data and noticed that it was mostly the regime driving those results, not the strategies themselves.

Also, how many strategies or variations did you test before landing on this one? Was it cherry-picked, or were the results consistently good without being too sensitive to small parameter changes?

Another thing: doubling the risk from 1% to 2% more than triples the profit. Are those exactly the same trades with different position sizes? Seems like quite a big difference, even with compounding.

Regarding Monte Carlo, it's definitely useful, but you're still working with the same historical trades. If the original results are overfitted, 5,000 simulations won't really tell you whether the edge is real.

And how much of the total profit comes from just a few big winners? The drawdown looks great, but 186 trades isn't exactly a huge sample.

I'm not saying any of this to weaken your results. Just a few things I'd revisit to make sure you've checked all the details. Really hope you've found something that works!

replies.author: CantaloupeEast6276
replies.body:
Really appreciate you taking the time to write such a detailed response. These are exactly the sorts of questions I've been trying to answer throughout development.

Firstly, January–October 2026 wasn't genuinely untouched out-of-sample data. It was part of the development and testing process, so I completely agree that overfitting is a potential concern.

Regarding the longer-term performance, I've backtested from November 2022 through to October 2026, covering approximately 982 trades. At 1% risk, the four-year test produced around $4,609 net profit from a $5,000 starting balance, with a profit factor of 1.38 and maximum equity drawdown of 8.13%.

So the strategy remained profitable over the longer period, but the performance was noticeably weaker than the 2026 results. A substantial proportion of the profits came from 2026, which is something I'm particularly conscious of when considering different market regimes.

In terms of development, I've run hundreds of backtests across multiple versions, changing individual parameters and comparing the results rather than adjusting everything simultaneously. I've also tested different commission and slippage assumptions, position sizing, risk limits and exit strategies. However, I recognise that repeatedly testing variations on the same historical data introduces selection bias, even when the changes are made systematically.

You've also spotted something interesting regarding the 1% versus 2% risk results. They weren't actually identical trade sets. At 1% risk, the bot executed 186 trades, whereas at 2% it executed 192. My suspicion is that the difference comes from minimum position sizes and the bot's strict monetary risk limits preventing certain trades at lower risk levels. That's something I'm still investigating rather than attributing the entire profit increase to compounding.

I also completely agree regarding Monte Carlo. I've run 5,000-iteration block-bootstrap simulations, but ultimately they're resampling historical trades, so they can't independently establish whether the underlying edge is genuine.

As for how much of the profit comes from a handful of large winners, that's another area I want to analyse in more detail. I haven't yet independently reconstructed the equity curve or measured exactly how much the largest winners contribute.

I'm not claiming I've developed a proven profitable system just yet. The backtesting has been encouraging, but I realise there's a big difference between producing good historical results and demonstrating a sustainable edge in live conditions.



I've actually just gone through the complete exported trade history to investigate your point about profits being concentrated in a handful of winners.

The export contains 976 completed trades, generating $4,606.47 net profit with a profit factor of 1.38.

The 10 biggest winners contributed $2,046.33, roughly 44% of the total net profit. However, removing those 10 trades would still leave $2,560.14 in profit.

Even removing the 20 biggest winning trades, the remaining 956 trades would still have generated $1,381.53 net profit, with a profit factor of approximately 1.11.

Removing the top 30 winners still leaves a small profit of $404.17, although removing the top 50 would make the overall result negative.

I've also reconstructed the closed-trade balance curve and calculated a maximum balance drawdown of approximately 7.20%.

The other interesting finding is that approximately 64% of the 4 year net profit came from 2026. The strategy was also profitable in 2023, 2024 and 2025, but with considerably weaker profit factors.

So you're absolutely right that the stronger market conditions in 2026 played a significant role. The strategy doesn't appear to rely entirely on just a few unusually large trades, but larger winners and the 2026 market environment clearly contributed substantially to its overall profitability. I do also think if it can be profitbale from the current year then it should survive overall. This year has been a \*\*\*\* for trading.

The strategy remained profitable across 2023, 2024 and 2025, although the profit factors were considerably lower than in 2026. Around 64% of the total four-year profit came from 2026, so there's definitely evidence that certain market conditions favour the strategy more than others.

That's why I've now moved into live forward testing. The historical results are encouraging, but I want to establish whether the edge remains consistent in changing market conditions before considering increasing the capital.

I certainly wouldn't consider it a proven strategy just yet!

comments.author: KoresignalAI
comments.body:
Nice work on the Monte Carlo, most people stop at one backtest. A few honest checks before getting excited:

- **Forward test on demo or tiny live size for 2-3 months.** Backtest fills on gold, especially around news, are often way kinder than reality.
- **Spread/slippage stress test:** rerun with 1.5-2x the spread. If PF drops below ~1.3, the edge is fragile.
- **Out-of-sample:** were the 2026 results part of the period you developed on? If yes, they're in-sample.
- **Equity DD vs balance DD gap** (4.52 vs 2.96 at 1%) suggests trades sit in drawdown a while; check the worst single-trade adverse move.

If it survives forward testing at small size, then scale slowly. Good luck!

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The live and backtest match on one trade is a good sign for the fills, but it says nothing about the edge. I'd check a few things next: whether the results hold on data the rules never saw (not just the four-year run you tuned on), how many versions and settings you tried along the way, and whether results hold with wider spreads and slippage, since gold spreads can jump around news. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to run that kind of out-of-sample check.

replies.author: CantaloupeEast6276
replies.body:
Really appreciate the feedback, and I completely agree with your points.

I've actually run hundreds of backtests across multiple versions and parameter combinations, using approximately four years of historical tick data covering 976 trades. I've generally changed one parameter at a time to compare the results, although I appreciate that repeatedly testing against the same dataset creates a risk of overfitting.

I've also stress-tested commission assumptions at $2, $10 and $25, alongside adverse slippage scenarios of $0.10, $0.25, $0.50 and $1.00 per fill. The strategy remained profitable under those tested assumptions, but I recognise that this doesn't fully replicate the spread widening and unpredictable execution that can occur around major news events.

And you're absolutely right about Monte Carlo. The 5,000 block-bootstrap simulations help assess drawdown and trade-sequencing risk, but they don't establish whether the strategy has a genuine edge outside the historical data.

The longer four-year backtest remained profitable, although 2026 accounted for approximately 64% of total profits, so market-regime dependence is something I'm particularly conscious of.

I've only just started running the bot live with real capital, and I'm deliberately keeping the risk controlled while collecting forward-testing data. 

I'll have a look at Cymetica's Backtest Labs as well. I'm keen to find ways of validating the strategy independently rather than just continuing to optimise it against the same historical dataset.

Thanks again, genuinely useful feedback!

comments.author: Wild-Raspberry-1770
comments.body:
This is actually one of the more interesting XAUUSD bot results I've seen here, particularly because you're testing with tick data, reporting Monte Carlo results, and already comparing live execution against your backtest.
I'm working on an independent quantitative research project . I've been investigating why apparently profitable strategies often fail when tested against stricter statistical and execution assumptions.
I'd be interested in offering you something in return for a little additional data: a free, independent forensic validation of your results.
And to be clear, i don't need your strategy logic, source code, indicators, parameters, or anything that would reveal your trading edge. Your intellectual property stays yours.
What would be genuinely useful is:
1. An anonymized trade export — timestamps, direction, entry/exit prices, position sizes, costs, and net P&L for the 186 trades.
2. The research timeline — when the current strategy was finalized, whether 2026 was genuinely untouched out-of-sample data, and roughly how many configurations were tested before arriving at this version.
3. Your Monte Carlo setup — block length, resampling assumptions, and the distribution of outcomes, especially drawdown and losing streaks.
4. The 1%, 1.5%, and 2% risk results — whether all three versions generated exactly the same trades or whether position sizing affected execution.
5. The first live/backtest comparison — anonymized execution details behind that impressive $0.12 difference.
Here's what we'd do with it:
- Independently reconstruct the equity curve and performance statistics.
- Test whether the results are concentrated in a handful of trades or market regimes.
- Stress-test spreads, slippage, and execution assumptions.
- Examine selection bias and the credibility of the out-of-sample period.
- Identify what the live/backtest comparison genuinely establishes.
You'd receive a concise independent assessment of what holds up, what remains uncertain, and what should be tested next — including negative findings.
I wouldn't publish your raw data or any identifying details without your explicit permission.
I think this could be mutually useful: you get another set of eyes on a strategy you've clearly put serious work into, and we get to test our research methodology against a real-world system rather than another hypothetical backtest.
Even if you're not comfortable sharing a full trade export, we could start with the strategy-finalization date, the number of configurations tested, and an anonymized monthly performance breakdown.
Would you be open to that?

comments.author: CantaloupeEast6276
comments.body:
Good questions, and are things I've been looking into.

The trade counts weren't identical. At 1% equity risk, the bot took 186 trades, compared with 192 at 2%, despite using the same strategy. I suspect this relates to position sizing, minimum trade volumes and risk restrictions, but I'm still investigating the exact differences.

Regarding the testing, I've backtested approximately 4 years, october 2022 - till present all on historical tick data, covering around 982 trades. I've also stress-tested commission assumptions at $2, $10 and $25, alongside adverse slippage scenarios of $0.10, $0.25, $0.50 and $1.00 per fill, applied to both entries and exits.

The slippage analysis was a historical sensitivity test using fixed 0.01-lot trades, rather than a full execution re-simulation. The strategy remained profitable under those tested assumptions.

As for January–October 2026, that wasn't a genuinely untouched out-of-sample period. It formed part of the development and testing process, so I'm not claiming otherwise.

The $0.12 difference came from a slightly worse closing price on the live trade compared with the backtest.

Both trades were identical on entry:

||Backtest|Live trade|
|:-|:-|:-|
|Entry price|$4,146.83|$4,146.83|
|Exit price|$4,121.16|$4,121.10|
|Position size|0.02 lots (2 oz)|0.02 lots (2 oz)|
|Net P&L|−$51.46|−$51.58|

The live exit was $0.06 per ounce worse.

Why did the closing prices differ? Most likely ordinary execution slippage or a slight difference in the bid quote when the bot closed the position at its scheduled time.

The entry prices matched exactly, and the closing executions were only about 0.23 seconds apart.

So the $0.12 wasn't an additional commission or a problem with the bot. It was a tiny difference in the price received when closing.

Without an air-gapped risk daemon, the first tail-risk event wipes out 6 months of paper profits."*
